synthesis.headline: The block's northern anchor lets go: a trough digs into the interior West as the heat ridge retreats to its Southwest/northern-Mexico core, focusing a multi-day rain-and-severe corridor across the central US
synthesis.narrative:
The high-amplitude summer block Tlaloc has tracked for more than three weeks has taken the decisive step its endgame promised. As recently as yesterday the western anchor was still a closed ridge sitting emphatically over the northern Rockies; today's 500 mb analysis shows that anchor gone. A deep, broadly amplified trough now runs from the Pacific Northwest through the central Rockies into the Desert Southwest, with the western anticyclone displaced southwest to the California coast and Nevada (a 600 dam ridge). A second subtropical ridge holds over the Southeast and Gulf Coast in the 588-594 dam range. The result is a ridge-trough-ridge across the CONUS with a shortwave dropping through southern Canada driving the day's action, rather than the near-stationary heat dome that defined the last three weeks. At the surface a sprawling low complex sits over the central High Plains and Rockies (primary center near 1006-1007 mb over eastern Colorado), with a warm front east across the mid-Missouri Valley and a cold front trailing south into Texas.

Today's busiest center of action is the central US. A slow-moving frontal boundary arcs from the mid-Mississippi Valley into the Tennessee Valley, and the warm sector beneath it — dewpoints in the upper 60s to mid 70s across Kansas and Missouri — is where lift is best organized. SPC carries a Slight Risk over the middle Mississippi Valley, with supercells possible over eastern Missouri, western Illinois, and southeast Iowa (damaging wind the primary hazard, some hail and a low-end tornado threat under 30-35+ kt shear), and WPC overlays a Slight Risk for excessive rainfall from the Upper Midwest through the mid-Mississippi and Ohio Valleys with flash-flood potential along the stalled boundary. That threat translates east on Saturday: SPC's Day 2 places a Slight Risk over central Kentucky, middle Tennessee, and northern Alabama, damaging wind again primary as a surface low tracks from Illinois toward southeast Michigan and a 30-35 kt low-level jet sharpens shear over the Ohio and Tennessee Valleys. Beneath the retreating western ridge, dangerous heat is building — highs of 110-120 across the Southwest, expanding into the northern High Plains and Intermountain West this weekend — while the North American Monsoon keeps a flash-flood and marginal-severe threat going over the Four Corners and New Mexico. Canada carries real weight: a broad low-pressure field dominates the central and eastern domain, and the cold front from the central Prairies south into the north-central US marks the continent's dominant forcing axis, while a strong 1038 hPa high off Labrador tightens the gradient into Atlantic Canada. Yesterday's exceptionally deep 979 hPa Ontario-Quebec cyclone has clearly filled and moved on.

Aloft the story is coherent. Air Mass RGB shows a broad dry, red-orange swath over the central and western CONUS — subsident mid-to-upper air under the summer ridge, not a stratospheric intrusion given its areal extent and its position away from any trough axis — with a sharp airmass boundary arcing from the upper Great Lakes southwest through the Ohio Valley toward the Gulf, marking the implied jet corridor; the organized convection from the Tennessee Valley into the Carolinas is firing on the moist tropical side of that boundary. Over Canada, the Hudson Bay airmass boundary traces the polar-jet corridor with cold, dry upper air to the north. The closed low plotted off the Northeast/Mid-Atlantic coast is a cutoff pivoting separately from the westerlies rather than translating downstream. The regime question — whether the western ridge regenerates over the north or genuinely retreats — is settled clearly by the ensemble pair. The 6-10 day (Aug 5-9) height outlook keeps the western positive anomaly modest (a few dam) with its zero line near the Rockies, not reaching the interior, and an eastern-Canada trough dominating; the 8-14 day (Aug 7-13) then places the 588-594 dam ridge core over the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico (594 dam near the Four Corners) with the northern Rockies, northern Plains, and western Canada left in a trough regime. The ridge contracts further southwest between the two leads — this is a genuine geographic retreat to its climatological home, not a cosmetic flattening and not a collapse. The 6-10 day temperature outlook corroborates, anchoring the hottest 90-100% probabilities over Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma, and northern Texas while the northern tier weakens. The teleconnection indices are a consistent directional cross-check on that height story, not its basis: PNA has firmed to +0.74 (western ridge/eastern trough), AO has surged to +0.95 (suppressed high-latitude blocking, favoring the more progressive northern-tier flow), and NAO has flipped to +0.71 — all rising, all pointing the same way as the fields.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-summer North America, with heat-and-severe season driving both the entrenched interior heat and the marginal severe threats ringing the retreating ridge, and the North American Monsoon in full swing over the Desert Southwest and southern Rockies feeding the Four Corners and New Mexico flash-flood threat. The ENSO backdrop remains one of steady cold-to-warm transition: after a weak La Niña through late 2025, the ONI warmed through neutral early in 2026 and reached +0.98 by April-June, indicating a developing El Niño that will increasingly shape steering and shear through the back half of the season. The hurricane basins stay split against the climatological ramp toward the September peak — the Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf are quiet with no development expected over the next seven days, while the East Pacific holds Tropical Storm Genevieve (weakened from hurricane strength yesterday) west of southern Baja California, with no additional formation anticipated.
synthesis.regional_notes: No SPC mesoscale discussions are active as of this briefing. Today's sharpest sub-synoptic signal is the supercell threat over eastern Missouri, western Illinois, and southeast Iowa this afternoon (hail, damaging winds, isolated tornado potential), plus a flash-flood axis from the Upper Midwest into the Ohio Valley along the stalled front; isolated severe wind and hail are also possible over the southern and central High Plains near terrain. Saturday the severe threat consolidates over central Kentucky, middle Tennessee, and northern Alabama, with a secondary High Plains/New Mexico-into-southeast Arizona threat from a weak disturbance and monsoon upslope flow. Major-to-extreme heat risk builds across the Southwest (110-120) and spreads into the northern High Plains and Intermountain West. In Canada, the Prairie cold front holds the tightest gradient inland, while the 1038 hPa Labrador high tightens winds across Atlantic Canada.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 1200Z 31 July 2026 WPC surface analysis shows a sprawling low pressure complex centered over the central High Plains and adjacent Rockies, with the primary center reading near 1006-1007 mb over roughly eastern Colorado and a secondary around 1013 mb farther south over the southern Plains, both linked by a continuous warm front extending eastward across the mid-Missouri Valley and a cold front trailing southward through the central and southern Plains into Texas. A well-defined stationary or slow-moving frontal boundary arcs across the mid-Mississippi Valley and into the Tennessee Valley, and the combination of the warm front to the north and this boundary to the east creates a pronounced moisture focus over the central U.S., where dewpoints in the upper 60s to mid-70s F are plotted alongside converging wind shifts — the surface pattern is clearly organizing lift along that frontal zone. The Pacific coast shows a tight gradient along the California and Oregon coast, consistent with a strong thermal trough or onshore flow regime, while a 1022 mb high anchors the interior Great Basin. Along the East Coast, gradients are slack between a modest Atlantic high near 1019-1021 mb and the inland low, offering little organized boundary forcing there; a weakening low near the Mid-Atlantic coast around 1013 mb introduces some convergence but the frontal definition there looks diffuse. The most energetic surface focus on this chart is the warm-sector moisture pool over Kansas, Missouri, and adjacent states, where the front geometry and low-level flow convergence are best positioned to support deep convective initiation.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z 31 July 2026 shows a broad area of low pressure dominating the central and eastern portions of the Canadian domain, with multiple weak lows and quasi-stationary frontal segments threading across the southern Prairies and into Ontario and Quebec; the tightest isobar packing on the Canadian side appears along a cold frontal boundary that extends from somewhere over the central Prairies southward into the north-central United States, implying the strongest surface pressure gradient and wind potential in that corridor. A prominent 1038 hPa high is centered well out over what appears to be the northwestern North Atlantic or Labrador Sea region based on its position relative to visible northeastern coastlines, and its southern flank is directing a tightening gradient into Atlantic Canada. Over the high Arctic portion of the chart, the upper frame carries several lows in the 986-997 hPa range, but given the polar projection these are positioned near or above 75-80N and should not be read as Canadian provincial systems. A complex of fronts and a slow-moving low near 1002-1009 hPa sits over what the coastline geometry suggests is somewhere in the vicinity of Hudson Bay or the Ontario-Manitoba border area, which would focus lift and moisture convergence across a broad swath of central Canada. Across the border into the northern United States, the frontal zone connecting to the Prairie system appears to be the dominant synoptic forcing axis, with Highs over the southeastern US at 1017-1018 hPa keeping the moisture return active on the warm side.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: Valid 1200 UTC 31 July 2026, this 500 mb analysis shows a broadly amplified longwave pattern across the contiguous United States. A deep trough axis runs roughly from the Pacific Northwest southward through the central Rockies and into the Desert Southwest, with heights falling to around 594 dam over the interior West and a broad ridge of 600 dam centered over the California coast and Nevada, placing the western anticyclone well to the southwest. To the east, heights rise into the 588-594 dam range across the Southeast and Gulf Coast, consistent with a second subtropical ridge. A concentrated region of negative 500 mb temperature anomaly (implied by the green shading and the labeled temperatures in the negative teens Celsius) coincides with the trough axis stretching from the Pacific Northwest southward into the central High Plains, and the trough's orientation appears to have a slight negative tilt across the Plains, with the base displaced eastward relative to the northern axis. A closed low marked with an "L" is plotted off the mid-Atlantic or Northeast coast at the chart's right edge, which if genuine would make it a cutoff feature pivoting separately from the main westerlies rather than translating downstream. Wind barbs in the green-shaded corridor suggest a jet streak implied along the trough axis oriented southwest to northeast across the northern Rockies into the Upper Midwest, while overall the broad ridge-trough-ridge pattern and the coastal cutoff low together suggest a somewhat blocked or retrogressive regime rather than progressive zonal flow.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 AirMass RGB from 31 July 2026 at 1401Z shows a broad red-orange swath covering most of the central and western contiguous United States, consistent with dry mid-to-upper-tropospheric air under what is likely a sprawling summer ridge; this is not a stratospheric intrusion signature given its areal extent and position away from any trough axis. A sharp, curving airmass boundary arcs from around the upper Great Lakes southwestward through the Ohio Valley and toward the central Gulf Coast states, where the red-orange dry air abruptly gives way to green moist tropical air to the south and east — this boundary marks the likely jet corridor implied by the contrast. Organized deep convection with bright white high tops is concentrated along and just south of that boundary from roughly the Tennessee Valley into the Carolinas, with an additional cluster over southern Georgia and northeastern Florida. A separate area of organized convection with a modest cold-top signature is visible over southern Mexico near the bottom of the frame, along with scattered deep cells across the Caribbean. The Atlantic off the mid-Atlantic and southeastern U.S. coast shows moist green tones with scattered convective cells but no organized tropical structure clearly discernible in this single frame.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 31 July 2026 at 1350Z shows a broad swath of red-orange coloring across the subtropical and tropical Pacific west of Mexico and extending into the interior western United States, consistent with dry, subsident upper-tropospheric air under a summer ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. The ITCZ is evident as a band of bright white convective tops and green moisture stretching across the eastern Pacific roughly 5-15 degrees north of the equator, with additional clusters of deep convection visible over Central America and the northern Amazon basin. In the Southern Hemisphere extratropics, two well-defined cyclonic swirl signatures appear in the South Atlantic and southern Pacific near the tip of South America, with the South Pacific system displaying a compact, elongated filament of saturated red-orange color wrapping into its center on the equatorward side, which is a credible stratospheric-intrusion signature given its position on the cyclonic side of Southern Hemisphere westerly flow. Across Canada, a sharp blue-green airmass boundary oriented roughly southwest to northeast through the Hudson Bay region marks the implied polar jet corridor, with cold dry upper-tropospheric blue tones dominating northern Canada and warmer airmass colors to the south. The Caribbean and tropical Atlantic appear largely cloud-free at upper levels with modest low-topped convection, showing no clear organized tropical wave signature at this valid time.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The chart valid August 5-9, 2026 shows above-normal temperatures favored across virtually the entire contiguous United States, with the highest probabilities — in the 90-100% range — concentrated in an elongated core stretching from the southern Rockies and high Plains of Colorado and Kansas southward into Oklahoma and northern Texas, implying a persistent and well-anchored upper-level ridge centered over that region. A secondary 80-90% probability area covers the Southeast from the Carolinas through Florida, while the northern tier from the Pacific Northwest through the northern Plains falls in the lower 40-50% range, suggesting the warm signal weakens considerably with distance from the ridge axis. The only below-normal signal visible on the conterminous map is essentially absent — there is no cool category shown over the Lower 48, meaning the pattern offers no meaningful escape from above-normal conditions anywhere in the contiguous states. The breadth and intensity of the above-normal probabilities, peaking at the highest confidence category over the central Rockies and southern Plains, are consistent with a persistent ridge rather than a transitional or breaking pattern; the gradient toward merely leaning-above across the Northwest hints at that flank being the most susceptible to any downstream shortwave intrusion, but the core signal does not support an imminent pattern breakdown within the valid period.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height anomaly forecast, valid August 5-9, 2026, made July 30, 2026. The dominant feature is a strongly negative anomaly center over the central Canadian Arctic, centered near Baffin Island or just west of it, where blue dashed contours indicate anomalies reaching -150 dam — that reading appears implausible for a 500 mb anomaly field; the contours labeled -90 and -150 most likely represent values in meters, so roughly -9 and -15 dam, which is a deep but physically reasonable cold trough anomaly. The associated 500 mb height low sits near 534-540 dam over the same region, with a broad trough axis dropping southward through eastern Canada toward the Great Lakes. Over the western contiguous United States and into the eastern Pacific, red dashed anomaly contours of +30 to +40 dam — again almost certainly meters, so +3 to +4 dam — suggest a modest positive anomaly ridge, but the zero line appears to fall near the Rockies or the western Plains, meaning the positive anomaly region does not extend deeply into the continental interior. The ridge axis over western North America is relatively flat and not strongly amplified; the overall pattern shows a downstream trough dominating the east while any western ridge is limited in both amplitude and eastward extent, implying flow that is trending toward modest amplification over the eastern part of the continent rather than a strongly meridional western ridge holding position.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly (departure from normal, dashed) prognostic valid 7–13 August 2026, made 30 July 2026 — consistent with CPC's 8–14 day product. The green solid contours show 500 mb heights at 60 m intervals, with values labeled in the 540–594 dam range across the domain; a closed low center sits over the central Canadian Arctic near Hudson Bay, with the 540 dam contour enclosing it, representing a strong negative height anomaly there. The dashed contours are the anomalies: a prominent positive anomaly center of roughly +8 to +9 dam (reading the dashed contours labeled near 90, which on the anomaly scale likely represents ~9 dam) is placed over the Canadian Arctic interior, but this appears to be the anomaly associated with the ridge wrapping around the low rather than a warm-core ridge — the dominant positive anomaly in the mid-latitudes is notably absent over western Canada and the northern Rockies. Instead, the 588–594 dam ridge axis is displaced well to the southwest, sitting over the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico, with the 594 dam contour centered near the Four Corners/northern Mexico region, indicating the ridge has retreated from the northern Rockies and northern Plains rather than sitting atop them. The northern Rockies, northern Plains, and western Canada fall in a trough regime behind the dominant flow, consistent with unseasonably cool and active conditions across that broad region during the valid period.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Upper-level shortwave trough moving through southern Canada drives unsettled conditions across central U.S. Friday through Sunday. Surface low deepens and moves eastward; frontal boundary extends across Mississippi Valley and Southern Plains. Slow-moving boundary interacting with warm moisture and strong instability produces heavy rainfall capable of flash flooding. Slight Risk excessive rainfall over Upper Midwest through mid-Mississippi Valley and Ohio Valley Friday; Slight Risk severe thunderstorms over Mississippi Valley and Ozarks. Saturday, system shifts eastward into Ohio/Tennessee Valley; severe risk and excessive rainfall risk shift into lower Great Lakes, Ohio/Tennessee Valley, and Southeast with potential damaging winds, hail, and possible tornadoes. Southwest monsoonal moisture brings afternoon-evening thunderstorms across Four Corners with flash flood and severe potential through Saturday. Dangerous heat builds Southwest Friday, northern High Plains and Intermountain West Saturday, with highs 110-120 degrees Southwest and 90s-100s northward; overnight relief minimal.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Slight Risk issued for middle Mississippi Valley. A positive-tilt trough moving southeast will bring a cold front across the lower Missouri Valley toward the Ozarks today. Fairly extensive elevated convection exists this morning across Missouri into western Illinois and eastern Iowa. Moderate to locally strong destabilization expected across central/southwest Missouri during peak heating as early clouds clear. Effective shear of 30-35 kt across Missouri Ozarks, stronger 40+ kt northward into Iowa/Illinois. Supercells possible; some hail likely, low-level shear supporting tornado potential mainly in eastern Missouri and nearby western Illinois/southeast Iowa. Damaging winds expected as primary severe threat spreading southeast through late afternoon/evening. Isolated severe storms also possible across southern Plains and central/southern High Plains this afternoon through early evening, primarily severe wind gusts and hail near terrain.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No active mesoscale discussion. There is currently no organized convective threat being monitored by the Storm Prediction Center.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days across the North Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf of America.

East Pacific: Tropical Storm Genevieve is currently being monitored west of southern Baja California. No additional tropical cyclone formation anticipated over the next 7 days in the eastern and central North Pacific east of 180 longitude.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: Cold anomalies persist through early 2026. The Oceanic Niño Index shows weak-to-moderate La Niña conditions currently (SON 2025 at -0.51), persisting through NDJ 2025 near -0.54. Anomalies gradually weaken through DJF 2026 and JFM 2026, transitioning to neutral in FMA 2026 (-0.14 to +0.13). Warming accelerates thereafter, with positive anomalies developing by MAM 2026 (+0.51) and strengthening into AMJ 2026 (+0.98), suggesting a shift toward El Niño conditions by late spring.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA has strengthened notably over the past week, rising from +0.44 to +0.74 (7-day means), supporting western ridging and eastern troughing. AO has surged from +0.22 to +0.95, indicating reduced high-latitude blocking. NAO has flipped decisively from -0.49 to +0.71, a swing of 1.19 standardized units, suggesting improved potential for eastern systems to escape. All three indices are rising. Note these are observed values in early summer when extratropical patterns are weaker than in winter; use as directional guidance rather than definitive evidence.
